torpid

TOR-pid · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Torpid is mentally or physically inactive; sluggish, dormant.

The old office computer felt torpid, taking nearly a minute just to open a single file.

Worked Example

The town's economy had grown torpid, with no new businesses opening in over a decade.

An economy with no new activity for a decade isn't just quiet -- it's stuck in an inactive, sluggish state, which is exactly torpid.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sluggish: Sluggish is the everyday word for slow and low on energy -- traffic crawling after an accident, a person before their first coffee. Torpid goes much deeper: so inactive that a body or mind seems nearly shut down, closer to a standstill than to ordinary slowness.

inactive: Inactive is the neutral, factual word for something not moving or operating at the moment -- a paused account, an idle machine. Torpid adds a heavy, sunk-in quality: not simply switched off, but slowed almost to a standstill and hard to rouse.

stagnant: Stagnant describes something that has stopped moving or developing and has gone stale from standing still -- a scummy pond, a debate that never advances. Torpid belongs to a living thing's own state: slowed almost to a standstill, sunk in heavy inactivity, yet able to revive.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

brisk: quick and energetic

Where it sits · how close to a complete standstill — slow → torpid → comatose

slow vs. torpid: Being slow just means reduced speed; being torpid means a much deeper sluggishness, close to complete inactivity.

comatose vs. torpid: A torpid creature is still capable of stirring eventually; a comatose one is completely unresponsive.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — torp

root — torp: to be numb or stiff (Latin (torpere))

suffix — -id

suffix — -id: having the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Torpid comes from Latin torpere, 'to be numb or stiff,' plus -id -- so torpid describes something that has gone numb and sluggish.

Use the root in a new word: torpedo

Use the root in a new word: torpedo: The same torpere root gives us torpedo -- the electric ray fish was named first, for the numbing shock it delivers, and the weapon was later named after the fish.

Word Choice

Torpid describes an inactive, shut-down state (an animal in hibernation, a stalled economy), distinct from this unit's "lassitude" (a personal, drained feeling) and "somnolence" (specifically about drowsiness).
